rows.reference: Bahá'u'lláh, Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶19 (paragraph numbering of the 1992 authorised translation)
rows.original: قد حرّم عليكم القتل والزّنا (qad ḥurrima ʿalaykum al-qatl wa'l-zinā)
rows.translation: Universal House of Justice, authorised translation (1992)
rows.says: "Ye have been forbidden to commit murder or adultery, or to engage in backbiting or calumny"; believers are then told to shun what the holy Books and Tablets forbid. The Arabic word rendered "murder" is al-qatl, the general noun for killing, from the same root (q-t-l) as "slay" in ¶73 and "take another's life" in ¶62 and ¶188. No class of victim is named or excepted, and the ban is not limited to fellow believers.
rows.bearing: K1: Taught (rule 7), Explicit. Tier 1, every branch, read directly. It forbids killing with no class of victim excepted, so it reaches everyone K1 protects, newborns included (rule 9), whatever their faith, sex or status. The only deliberate killing the Aqdas provides for is the penalty of ¶62, a court matter (rule 5). A total ban contains K1; it need not state K1's defence exception. K0: Taught a fortiori. K3: does not speak of war; Implied at most.

rows.reference: Bahá'u'lláh, Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶73 (paragraph number confirmed; it follows the ban on slave trading in ¶72)
rows.original: لا يعترض احد على احد ولا يقتل نفس نفساً ... اتقتلون من احياه الله بروح من عنده (wa-lā yaqtul nafsun nafsan ... a-taqtulūna man aḥyāhu'llāh)
rows.translation: Universal House of Justice, authorised translation (1992)
rows.says: Believers are told to adorn themselves with good deeds and to aid the Cause by righteous works, wisdom and utterance. Then: "Let none contend with another, and let no soul slay another", a ban said to have been laid down in a Book long concealed. It asks: "Would ye kill him whom God hath quickened", whom God endowed with spirit through His breath, calls this a grievous trespass, and forbids lifting the hand of injustice and oppression to destroy what God has raised up.
rows.bearing: K1: Taught (rule 7), Explicit. A second Tier 1 text, every branch, read directly. "No soul shall kill a soul" names no excepted class, and the reason given (God gave every person life and spirit) applies to every person from birth onwards (rule 9). K0: Taught a fortiori. K3: does not mention war; Implied. Correction to the earlier note: it is not stronger than ¶19 because it says "slay"; the Arabic of both uses the same root q-t-l, and the difference lies only in the English.

rows.reference: Bahá'u'lláh, Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶148
rows.original: قد منعتم في الكتاب عن الجدال والنّزاع والضّرب ... لا ترضوا لاحد ما لا ترضونه لانفسكم
rows.translation: Universal House of Justice, authorised translation (1992)
rows.says: Forbids believers "to engage in contention and conflict, to strike another", or anything similar that saddens hearts. A former fine of nineteen mithqáls of gold for saddening another is lifted in this Dispensation. It ends: "Wish not for others what ye wish not for yourselves".
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a wider duty (rule 7). A ban on striking anyone (al-ḍarb) reaches the graver act of killing and names no household, faith or status exception. The House of Justice letter of 24 January 1993 reads the striking ban as allowing gentle physical discipline of children; that concerns light correction, not killing, so it raises no rule 6 issue. K3: no bearing. Not needed for the label, since ¶19 and ¶73 are Explicit.

rows.reference: Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh, CXXVIII
rows.says: "Say: Fear God, O people, and refrain from shedding the blood of any one. Contend not with your neighbor". Believers are told not to commit disorders on the earth after it has been well ordered, to be fair to themselves and others, and that the Cause must be taught through utterance, "not through resort to violence". The section opens with the question whether one who claims to follow the All-Merciful may do the deeds of the Evil One; Epistle ¶91 opens with the same question and gives the same ban, so the two seem to render one tablet and are not independent witnesses.
rows.bearing: K1: Taught (rule 7), Explicit. Tier 1, every branch, read directly. "Any one" is universal: no class of victim is excepted. K0: Taught a fortiori. K3: does not mention war; Implied.

rows.reference: Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh, CXXXIX (to Nabíl-i-Aʿẓam) and CLIV (to Salmán)
rows.says: CXXXIX: "We have annulled the rule of the sword, as an aid to Our Cause", and replaced it with the power of human utterance; people are not to sow discord or contend with their neighbours. CLIV: those who attack the Faith in their writings are to be answered by refuting their arguments; whoever wishes to promote the Cause must do so "through his pen and tongue, rather than have recourse to sword or violence".
rows.bearing: K1: Clear teaching that no believer may use violence, still less kill, to serve or defend the religion, even against those who assail it. This is the Bahá'í answer to the zealot case (compare Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31, or Abū Dāwūd 4361): the founder forbids it rather than rewarding it. K0: supports (no killing out of religious hatred). K3: abolishes religious war only; Implied.

rows.reference: ʿAbdu'l-Bahá, Some Answered Questions, chapter on the punishment of criminals ("The Right Method of Treating Criminals" in the 1908 and 1990 editions; "The Punishment of Criminals" in the 2014 revised translation). Chapter number not confirmed (77 by the researchers' count; the web page name is SAQ-78).
rows.translation: L. C. Barney (1908, public domain) and the 2014 revised translation; wording below from search summaries of both
rows.says: There are two kinds of retribution, revenge and punishment. The individual has no right to revenge: "The wronged and aggrieved party has no right to seek revenge" and should show forgiveness and magnanimity. The body politic may punish the criminal, without hatred, to protect people's rights and deter others. What matters most is to educate people so that crimes are not committed.

It is the tradition's counted reading that places ¶62 with the community and its institutions. No dispute about this within the tradition was found, so rule 6 does not apply. Counted for every branch (rule 1).
rows.strength: Explicit (K0, revenge clause); Clear teaching (K1, no private authority to kill)

rows.reference: Bahá'u'lláh, Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶62 (arson and murder)
rows.original: ومن قتل نفساً عامداً فاقتلوه ... وان تحكموا لهما حبساً ابديّاً لا بأس عليكم (wa-man qatala nafsan ʿāmidan fa-qtulūhu)
rows.translation: Universal House of Justice, authorised translation (1992)
rows.says: Whoever intentionally burns a house is to be burned; "should anyone deliberately take another's life, him also shall ye put to death". Believers are told to hold fast to God's precepts and abandon the ways of the ignorant. Condemning the arsonist and the murderer to life imprisonment is also permissible under the Book. The command is in the plural ("ye") and the text does not itself name who carries it out.
rows.bearing: Court punishment: context only, exclusion (a) (rule 5). The text names no kinsman, victim's family or private avenger (contrast Numbers 35:26 to 27, where the text itself names the kinsman). The tradition's counted reading (Some Answered Questions, row 10) denies the wronged party any right to revenge and gives punishment to the body politic; the House of Justice (1967 letter, row 19, Tier 2) draws the same line; Notes 86 and 87 leave degrees of guilt and the choice of penalty to the House of Justice. No Bahá'í reading of ¶62 as a private licence was found, so rule 6 does not apply. It treats deliberate killing as among the gravest crimes, which is consistent with ¶19 and ¶73.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (direct, bahaiwritings): writings/aqdas.json paragraph 62, English and Arabic; seen: "should anyone deliberately take another's life, him also shall ye put to death" and "ومن قتل نفساً عامداً فاقتلوه".
rows.check: read directly and corrected: ¶62's own wording and Arabic now seen (earlier only through the Notes and search summaries); the recalled transliteration matches.

The claim that these Notes present the penal laws as meant for a future state of society is not in the record of what was seen and remains unverified.

rows.says: Bahá'ís recognise the right and duty of governments to use force to keep order and protect their people. The Faith "draws a very definite distinction between the duty of an individual to forgive and 'to be killed rather than to kill' and the duty of society to uphold justice", as ʿAbdu'l-Bahá explains in Some Answered Questions. Bahá'ís are not absolute pacifists, but try to avoid shedding blood in the world's conflicts.

That supports placing ¶62 under rule 5 and confirms the content of row 10. Tier 2: it cannot decide (decision 8). K3: context only; it does not address people who are not fighting.

rows.reference: Bahá'u'lláh, Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶37
rows.original: وان اصرّ على ما قال يبعث عليه من لا يرحمه انّه شديد العقاب
rows.translation: Universal House of Justice, authorised translation (1992)
rows.says: Anyone who claims a direct revelation before a full thousand years is a lying impostor. God is asked to help him retract and will forgive him if he repents; if he persists, "God will, assuredly, send down one who will deal mercilessly with him" (Arabic: He will raise up against him one who will not show him mercy). Gleanings CXIX (read directly) commands the rulers to 'rise ye all against' any ruler who takes up arms, calls this 'manifest justice', and allows armaments to safeguard territories. So the general bans (¶19, ¶73, CXXVIII, Epistle ¶42) are not read as ruling out all war. No counted text found says whether, in such permitted force, people who are not fighting remain protected. objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The ¶19 row calls the ban total ('A total ban contains K1'), and the corrections propose noting in translations.md that 'murder' narrows the Arabic al-qatl. But ¶62, read directly, commands killing with the same root ('من قتل نفساً عامداً فاقتلوه', fa-qtulūhu). So in the Book's own terms al-qatl in ¶19 cannot mean every killing. It means unlawful killing, which is exactly what the authorised 'murder' says. The same holds for ¶73 ('let no soul slay another') and for 'shed not the blood of any one'. Universality therefore cannot rest on the word. It rests on two facts. First, the bans name no excepted class of victim, and the Epistle and Gleanings CXXVIII say 'any one'. Second, every exception the tradition's own texts recognise falls within K1's exclusions or its defence exception: the court penalty (¶62), collective force against an aggressor (Gleanings CXIX and CXVII), arms 'unless essential' (¶159), and defence of life when no authority is at hand (Lights 398 to 400, Tier 2). As written, the K1 reason treats the bans as total, while the K3 reason treats the same bans as narrowed by CXIX. Both cannot be right.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 and METHOD.md section 3, 'Wider rules': a general ban counts only as far as it reaches the protected class, so its recognised exceptions must be checked. Rule 5 (exclusions a and b). Consistency with general bans that carry an exception for lawful killing elsewhere, for example Qur'an 17:33 (read directly, Pickthall): 'slay not the life which Allah hath forbidden save with right'.
objections.proposed: Keep K1 Taught, Explicit. Reword the reason: 'general bans on wrongful killing that except no class of victim; the only killings the tradition's own texts allow are a court penalty, collective force against an aggressor and defence at need, all outside what K1 forbids'. In translations.md, record that al-qatl is the general word, but that the Book's own ¶62 shows ¶19 means unlawful killing. The authorised 'murder' is therefore a fair rendering, not a narrowing.

But every killing the tradition's own texts allow lies within K1's exclusions or its exception: a court penalty (¶62), collective force against an aggressor (Gleanings CXIX and CXVII), and arms at need (¶159; Tier 2 Lights 398 to 400 on defence of life). Rule 5: ¶62 is plural and names no executor. Unlike Qur'an 17:33 ('We have given power unto his heir') and Numbers 35:26 to 27, it gives no heir or kinsman any role, and ¶188 names the family only as receivers of an indemnity. ʿAbdu'l-Bahá (Some Answered Questions, counted, search-level) denies the wronged party any right of revenge and gives punishment to the body politic. The House of Justice (Lights 1354, direct) draws the same line. No dispute about this was found, so rule 6 does not apply. Zealot cases are condemned, not rewarded: Epistle ¶32 to ¶33 ('that evil deed'), Gleanings CXXXIX and CLIV (pen and tongue, not sword), and CXIII ('Will ye slay a man because he saith my Lord is God'). ¶37 foretells that God will raise up a merciless agent, possibly human, against a persistent false claimant, but names no killing and licenses no believer (rule 4). challenge.consistency_notes: Numbers 35:26 to 27 (Judaism and Christianity): that text names a private kinsman, and Qur'an 17:33 gives the heir power. Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶62 names neither, so it is treated as a court penalty under rule 5, and this rests on the Tier 1 text itself. Phinehas (Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31): the Bahá'í counterparts are condemned, not rewarded. These are the 1852 attempt on the Sháh (Epistle ¶32 to ¶33), religious violence in general (Gleanings CXXXIX, CLIV and CXIII; ¶73 in its setting of how to aid the Cause), and the 1872 ʿAkká killings (Tier 2, God Passes By). Abū Dāwūd 4361: no counted Bahá'í text declares any killing blameless because of who the victim is. ¶72 abolishes the slave trade and ¶188 sets one ungraded indemnity. Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2: Some Answered Questions chapter 7 calls burying daughters alive barbarism. ʿAbdu'l-Bahá's 'better a babe did not live than grow ignorant' (Lights 486) is hyperbole that licenses no act, so it is Implied (rule 4). Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra on the icchantika: the nearest Bahá'í analogue is ¶37 (the false claimant). It foretells a merciless agent raised by God on the model of Qur'an 7:167, but names no killing and licenses no one, so it is Implied (rule 4). Yasna 31.18 and 33.2, and the Atharvaveda rites: Prayers and Meditations LXXIII is a petition. It does ask that believers 'prevail', so the draft's contrast ('asks God to act') needs correcting. But it names no killing, and Tier 1 limits the means (CXXXIX, CLIV), so it is Implied. Two consistency flags. (1) The Báb's writings are Tier 1 for every Bahá'í branch, and their laws are held superseded. Christianity still weighs Old Testament laws that most Christians hold superseded, so supersession should not neutralise a verified Bábí licence for Bahá'ís unless the same rule applies to Christianity. Today no Bábí locus is verified. (2) For K3, use one cross-tradition test. Taught: the general ban stands and the war exception is limited to those who fight. Unclear: the exception's reach is undefined and a counted text or authorised reading narrows the ban for collective force (the Bahá'í case). Silent: no counted text bears on it. The same test should apply to any ahiṃsā tradition that also accepts royal or defensive war.
